content: Telluric acid is a chemical compound with the molecular formula Te(OH)₆. It exists as a white solid composed of octahedral Te(OH)₆ molecules, and this molecular structure remains intact when dissolved in water. There are two crystalline forms of telluric acid: rhombohedral and monoclinic, both of which also consist of octahedral Te(OH)₆ molecules. Telluric acid is classified as a weak acid and is dibasic, meaning it can donate two protons. It reacts with strong bases to form tellurate salts. Telluric acid can be synthesized through the oxidation of tellurium or tellurium dioxide using strong oxidizing agents such as hydrogen peroxide, chromium trioxide, or sodium peroxide. It exhibits oxidizing properties, as evidenced by its electrode potential, although its oxidation reactions proceed at a slow kinetic rate. The anhydrous form of telluric acid is stable in air at temperatures up to 100°C. However, when heated above this temperature, it undergoes dehydration to form polymetatelluric acid, a white hygroscopic powder with an approximate composition of (H₂TeO₄)₁₀, and allotelluric acid, which is a syrupy acid of unknown structure with an approximate composition of (H₂TeO₄)₃(H₂O)₄. When subjected to strong heating at temperatures exceeding 300°C, telluric acid decomposes to produce the α-crystalline form of tellurium trioxide (α-TeO₃). Reaction with diazomethane yields the hexamethyl ester, Te(OMe)₆. Telluric acid and its salts predominantly feature hexacoordinate tellurium atoms. This structural characteristic is observed even in salts such as magnesium tellurate (MgTeO₄), which is isostructural with magnesium molybdate and contains TeO₆ octahedra. Metatelluric acid (H₂TeO₄), the tellurium analogue of sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), has not been observed or characterized. Allotelluric acid, with an approximate composition of (H₂TeO₄)₃(H₂O)₄, is poorly characterized and may represent a mixture of Te(OH)₆ and polymeric forms of (H₂TeO₄)n. Tellurous acid (H₂TeO₃) is known to exist, but it is also not well characterized.
